arrays-hashing.title: A hash map answers "have I seen it?" in one step

frames.caption: Find two numbers that add up to 9. Instead of trying every pair, walk the array once and keep a hash map of what you have seen.
i = 0: x = 2, so it needs 7. Ask the map: is 7 there? No — one step, no second loop.
Now remember 2: store 2 → 0. Store after asking, so a number can never pair with itself.
i = 1: x = 7, so it needs 2. Is 2 in the map? Yes, at index 0.
Answer: [0, 1]. One pass and one map lookup per number: O(n) time, O(n) space, instead of O(n²) for every pair.
Put every number in a set: "is n in it?" now takes one step. The set has no order — it is drawn in order here only so runs are easy to see.
100: 99 is not in the set, so 100 starts a run. Count up: 100 → length 1.
4: is 3 in the set? Yes, so 4 is not the start of a run. Skip it — its run is counted from the start.
200: 199 is not in the set, so 200 starts a run. Count up: 200 → length 1.
1: 0 is not in the set, so 1 starts a run. Count up: 1, 2, 3, 4 → length 4.
3: is 2 in the set? Yes, so 3 is not the start of a run. Skip it — its run is counted from the start.
2: is 1 in the set? Yes, so 2 is not the start of a run. Skip it — its run is counted from the start.
Answer: 4. Counting only from starts means each number is looked at a handful of times, so the whole thing is O(n) — no sorting needed.

two-pointers.title: Two pointers: start at both ends, and each step rules out an answer

frames.caption: The array is sorted. Put L on the smallest number and R on the largest.
1 + 11 = 12: too big. L already holds the smallest number left, so 11 is too big with every partner. Drop it: move R left.
1 + 8 = 9: too small. R already holds the largest number left, so 1 is too small with every partner. Drop it: move L right.
2 + 8 = 10. Answer (1-indexed): [2, 5]. Each step threw away a number that could never be in the answer, so it is one pass and O(1) space.
Each number is a wall. Water between two walls is as high as the SHORTER wall, times the distance between them. Start with the widest pair.
min(1, 7) × 8 = 8. The left wall (1) is shorter, so it limits every container it is in. Moving the taller wall can never help: move L.
min(8, 7) × 7 = 49: the best so far. Now the right wall is shorter (or equal): move R.
min(8, 3) × 6 = 18. Best is still 49. Move the shorter wall: R.
min(8, 8) × 5 = 40. Best is still 49. Move the shorter wall: R.
min(8, 4) × 4 = 16. Best is still 49. Move the shorter wall: R.
min(8, 5) × 3 = 15. Best is still 49. Move the shorter wall: R.
min(8, 2) × 2 = 4. Best is still 49. Move the shorter wall: R.
min(8, 6) × 1 = 6. Best is still 49. Move the shorter wall: R.

L and R have met, so every pair worth checking has been checked. The best was walls 8 and 7, shown here: answer 49. One pass, because every move dropped a wall that could not be in a bigger container.

sliding-window.title: Sliding window: grow the right edge, shrink the left while the rule breaks

variants.label: Best Time to Buy and Sell

frames.caption: Buy on one day, sell on a later day. L is the buy day, R the sell day. Both edges only ever move right.
Day 1 costs £1, cheaper than buying on day 0 (£7). Any later sale does better from here, so move L to day 1.
L jumps to day 1: the new cheapest buy day.
Sell on day 2: £5 − £1 = £4. Best so far: £4.
Sell on day 3: £3 − £1 = £2. Best so far: £4.
Sell on day 4: £6 − £1 = £5. Best so far: £5.
Sell on day 5: £4 − £1 = £3. Best so far: £5.
Answer: £5 (buy at £1 on day 1, sell at £6 on day 4). One pass, O(n).
Find the longest stretch with no repeated letter. The window [L, R] only ever holds letters that are all different.
Add 'a': no repeat, so the window grows to 'a'.
Add 'b': no repeat, so the window grows to 'ab'.
Add 'c': no repeat, so the window grows to 'abc'.
Add 'a': but 'a' is already in the window. The window breaks the rule — shrink it from the left.
Drop 'a' from the left until 'a' is no longer repeated. Window: 'bca'. Best stays 3.
Add 'b': but 'b' is already in the window. The window breaks the rule — shrink it from the left.
Drop 'b' from the left until 'b' is no longer repeated. Window: 'cab'. Best stays 3.
Add 'c': but 'c' is already in the window. The window breaks the rule — shrink it from the left.
Drop 'c' from the left until 'c' is no longer repeated. Window: 'abc'. Best stays 3.
Add 'b': but 'b' is already in the window. The window breaks the rule — shrink it from the left.
Drop 'a' and 'b' from the left until 'b' is no longer repeated. Window: 'cb'. Best stays 3.
Add 'b': but 'b' is already in the window. The window breaks the rule — shrink it from the left.
Drop 'c' and 'b' from the left until 'b' is no longer repeated. Window: 'b'. Best stays 3.
Answer: 3. Each letter enters the window once and leaves at most once, so it is O(n), not O(n²).

stack.title: A stack: the most recent unfinished thing is resolved first

frames.caption: Every closing bracket must match the most recent opening bracket that is still open. "Most recent first" is exactly what a stack gives you.
'(' opens something: push it on the stack. It waits for its match.
'[' opens something: push it on the stack. It waits for its match.
']' closes something. The top of the stack is '[' — a match, so pop it.
'{' opens something: push it on the stack. It waits for its match.
'}' closes something. The top of the stack is '{' — a match, so pop it.
')' closes something. The top of the stack is '(' — a match, so pop it.
End of the string and the stack is empty: every bracket was matched in the right order. Answer: True. (A leftover item, or a mismatch on top, would mean False.)
For each day, how many days until it is warmer? Keep a stack of days still waiting. Their temperatures always go down from bottom to top.

binary-search.title: Binary search: each look throws away half of what is left

frames.caption: The array is sorted. Keep a range [lo, hi] that must contain the target, and look at the middle.
mid = (0 + 5) // 2 = 2, value 3. 3 < 9, and the array is sorted, so everything left of mid is too small as well.
Throw away the whole left half in one step: lo = mid + 1 = 3. Half the array gone with one comparison.
mid = (3 + 5) // 2 = 4, value 9. Found it: answer 4.
Two looks instead of five. Each look halves the range, so n items take about log₂ n looks: a million items, about 20.
Koko needs a speed k. Too slow and she runs out of time; any faster speed also works. So the speeds 1–11 are "sorted" by yes/no — search them by halving.

shapes.text: speed k (bananas per hour), must finish in h = 8 hours

frames.caption: Try k = 6: 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6 hours. Fast enough — but maybe slower also works: hi = 6.

shapes.text: speed k (bananas per hour), must finish in h = 8 hours

linked-list.title: Linked lists: rewire the arrows, and keep a pointer to what you would lose

frames.caption: Each node only knows the node after it. To reverse the list, walk it once and flip each arrow to point backwards. prev starts at None, curr at the head.
Save nxt = curr.next (2) first — otherwise flipping the arrow would lose the rest of the list.
curr.next = prev: 1 now points back to None. Then step forward: prev = 1, curr = 2.
Save nxt = curr.next (3) first — otherwise flipping the arrow would lose the rest of the list.
curr.next = prev: 2 now points back to 1. Then step forward: prev = 2, curr = 3.
Save nxt = curr.next (4) first — otherwise flipping the arrow would lose the rest of the list.
curr.next = prev: 3 now points back to 2. Then step forward: prev = 3, curr = 4.
Save nxt = curr.next (None) first — otherwise flipping the arrow would lose the rest of the list.
curr.next = prev: 4 now points back to 3. Then step forward: prev = 4, curr = None.
curr is None: done. prev is the new head. Answer: [4, 3, 2, 1]. One pass, O(n) time, and only three extra pointers, O(1) space.
Remove the 2nd node from the end. Add a dummy node D before the head, so even the head could be removed the same way. Both pointers start at D.
Move fast n + 1 = 3 steps ahead. Now the gap between them is 3, and it never changes.
Move both one step: slow → 1, fast → 4. The gap stays 3.
Move both one step: slow → 2, fast → 5. The gap stays 3.
Move both one step: fast falls off the end (None). Because the gap is 3, slow is now exactly one node BEFORE the one to remove.
slow.next = slow.next.next: 3 now points past 4 to 5. Answer: [1, 2, 3, 5]. One pass, no counting the length first.

trees.title: Trees: let each node ask its children, or visit level by level

frames.caption: How deep is the tree? Ask each node: "how deep is the tree below you?" A node waits for both children to answer, then returns 1 + the bigger answer. An empty child returns 0.
9 is a leaf: both children are empty (0). It returns 1 + max(0, 0) = 1.
15 is a leaf: both children are empty (0). It returns 1 + max(0, 0) = 1.
7 is a leaf: both children are empty (0). It returns 1 + max(0, 0) = 1.
20 has heard from both children: left 1, right 1. It returns 1 + max(1, 1) = 2.
3 has heard from both children: left 1, right 2. It returns 1 + max(1, 2) = 3.
The root returns 3: the answer. Children answer before parents (post-order), and each node is visited once: O(n).
Breadth-first: visit the tree one level at a time, using a queue (first in, first out). Start with just the root in the queue.
The queue holds exactly one level: [3]. Note its size (1) — that is how many to take out for this level.
Take out those 1, add them to the result as one list, and put their children in the queue: [9, 20].
The queue holds exactly one level: [9, 20]. Note its size (2) — that is how many to take out for this level.
Take out those 2, add them to the result as one list, and put their children in the queue: [15, 7].
The queue holds exactly one level: [15, 7]. Note its size (2) — that is how many to take out for this level.
Take out [15, 7]. They have no children, so the queue is empty: done.
Answer: [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]. Every node goes into the queue once and out once: O(n). Swap the queue for a stack and you get depth-first order instead.

heap-priority-queue.title: A heap keeps the biggest (or smallest) item on top

frames.caption: Each turn, smash the two heaviest stones. A max-heap keeps the heaviest at the top, always. Python's heapq is a min-heap, so the code stores −weight.
heapify arranges them as a tree where every parent is heavier than its children — in O(n). The heaviest, 8, is at the top.
Pop twice: 8 and 7, the two heaviest. After each pop the heap moves the next heaviest to the top, in O(log n).
8 − 7 = 1: push 1 back. It goes in at the bottom and swaps upwards only while it is heavier than its parent: O(log n).
Pop twice: 4 and 2, the two heaviest. After each pop the heap moves the next heaviest to the top, in O(log n).
4 − 2 = 2: push 2 back. It goes in at the bottom and swaps upwards only while it is heavier than its parent: O(log n).
Pop twice: 2 and 1, the two heaviest. After each pop the heap moves the next heaviest to the top, in O(log n).
2 − 1 = 1: push 1 back. It goes in at the bottom and swaps upwards only while it is heavier than its parent: O(log n).
Pop twice: 1 and 1, the two heaviest. After each pop the heap moves the next heaviest to the top, in O(log n).
1 and 1 are equal: both are destroyed, nothing goes back.
One stone left: answer 1. Each turn costs O(log n) instead of re-sorting the whole pile.
The 2nd largest number. Keep a MIN-heap of the 2 largest seen so far. Its top is the smallest of them — exactly the 2nd largest.
Push 3. The heap holds 1 of the 2 it is allowed: keep going.
Push 2. The heap holds 2 of the 2 it is allowed: keep going.
Push 1. Now there are 3 in the heap — one too many.
Pop the smallest (1): it cannot be among the 2 largest. The heap is back to 2: [2, 3].
Push 5. Now there are 3 in the heap — one too many.
Pop the smallest (2): it cannot be among the 2 largest. The heap is back to 2: [3, 5].
Push 6. Now there are 3 in the heap — one too many.
Pop the smallest (3): it cannot be among the 2 largest. The heap is back to 2: [5, 6].
Push 4. Now there are 3 in the heap — one too many.
Pop the smallest (4): it cannot be among the 2 largest. The heap is back to 2: [5, 6].
Answer: the top of the heap, 5. The heap never holds more than k items, so each step is O(log k) — better than sorting everything when k is small.

backtracking.title: Backtracking: choose, explore, un-choose — and prune dead ends

frames.caption: Every subset is a list of yes/no choices. Start with the empty path []. Record it — every path is a subset, not just the full ones.
Add 1: path [1]. Record it. Then try each later number: 2, 3.
Add 2: path [1, 2]. Record it. Then try each later number: 3.
Add 3: path [1, 2, 3]. Record it. No later numbers to add → undo the last choice and go back up.
Add 3: path [1, 3]. Record it. No later numbers to add → undo the last choice and go back up.
Add 2: path [2]. Record it. Then try each later number: 3.
Add 3: path [2, 3]. Record it. No later numbers to add → undo the last choice and go back up.
Add 3: path [3]. Record it. No later numbers to add → undo the last choice and go back up.
All 8 subsets: [[], [1], [1, 2], [1, 2, 3], [1, 3], [2], [2, 3], [3]]. Choose, explore, un-choose. Only trying LATER numbers stops [2, 1] repeating [1, 2].
Find every combination of 2, 3 and 5 that adds up to 8 (each number can be reused). Each circle is the running total of one path.
Keep choosing 2: totals 2, 4, 6, 8. Total = 8 is a hit: record [2, 2, 2, 2].
Back up to 6 and try 3 (total 9) and 5 (total 11): both over 8. Stop each one at once — that is the pruning.
Back up to 4 and choose 3 (total 7). Adding 3 or 5 overshoots: prune both.
From 4, choose 5: total 9, over. Prune. Everything under [2, 2] is done.
Back to [2], choose 3 (total 5), then 3 again: total 8, a hit. Record [2, 3, 3].
[2, 3, 5] is over. Then [2, 5] (total 7) and [2, 5, 5] (total 12): over. Branch [2] is finished.
Branch [3] only tries 3 and 5 — never 2 again, which is what stops [3, 2, 3] repeating [2, 3, 3]. [3, 3] then overshoots both ways.
[3, 5]: total 8, a hit. Record it.
Branch [5] can only add 5: total 10, over. The search is complete.
Answer: [[2, 2, 2, 2], [2, 3, 3], [3, 5]]. Green = hit, red = pruned the moment the total passed 8. Pruning early is what keeps backtracking fast enough.

tries.title: A trie: words stored letter by letter, sharing their starts

frames.caption: A trie stores words letter by letter along paths from the root. Words that share a start share a path. It starts as just the root.
insert 'app': create a → p → p, then mark the last p as the end of a word (green ring).

shapes.text: ◯ green ring = end of a word

frames.caption: insert 'apple': a → p → p already exist — walk them. Create only l → e, and mark e as a word end.

shapes.text: ◯ green ring = end of a word

frames.caption: search('app'): follow a → p → p. The last p has the word-end ring: True.

shapes.text: ◯ green ring = end of a word

frames.caption: search('ap'): follow a → p. The path exists, but this p has no word-end ring — 'ap' was never inserted: False.

shapes.text: ◯ green ring = end of a word

frames.caption: startsWith('ap'): follow a → p. The path exists, and that is all a prefix check needs: True.

shapes.text: ◯ green ring = end of a word

frames.caption: search('apt'): follow a → p, then look for 't'. There is no such child: False. It took 3 steps, not a scan of every word.

shapes.text: ◯ green ring = end of a word

frames.caption: Results: True, False, True, False. Each lookup costs the length of the word, however many words are stored.

shapes.text: ◯ green ring = end of a word

frames.caption: The words bad, dad and mad in a trie. A '.' in a search matches any one letter, so at a '.' the search must try every child.
.ad: the first letter is '.', so try each child in turn. The first, b, leads to a → d, a word end: True. The search stops at the first success.
b..: follow b. Then '.': try each child of b — just a. Then '.' again: try a's children — just d, a word end: True.
pa.: the root has no child 'p'. A plain letter that is missing ends the search at once: False.
Results: True, True, False. Plain letters follow one path; each '.' branches out — a small depth-first search inside the trie.

frames.caption: An arrow a → b means "take a before b". "in" counts how many prerequisites a course still needs. Courses needing none are ready: put them in a queue.
Take course 0. Cross out its arrows: 1 and 2 each need one fewer. 1 and 2 are now at 0: ready.
Take course 1. Cross out its arrows: 3 each need one fewer. Nothing new is ready yet.
Take course 2. Cross out its arrows: 3 each need one fewer. 3 is now at 0: ready.
Take course 3. It unlocks nothing — the queue is empty.
All 4 courses were taken, so there is no cycle: True — an order exists: [0, 1, 2, 3]. Each course and arrow is handled once: O(V + E).
Now a broken plan: 1 needs 0 and 2, but 2 needs 1. Only course 0 needs nothing, so only 0 is ready.
Take 0. Course 1 now needs one fewer — but it still waits for 2, and 2 waits for 1. Neither will ever reach 0.
The queue is empty but only 1 of 3 courses were taken. Courses stuck above 0 mean a cycle: False.

advanced-graphs.title: Weighted graphs: settle the closest first, or relax in rounds

frames.caption: A signal starts at node 2. How long until every node hears it? Dijkstra: always settle the closest node not yet settled. A heap keeps the closest on top.
Pop (0, 2): the closest unsettled node. Its time is final: 0. Push its neighbours: 1 at 0 + 1 = 1, 3 at 0 + 1 = 1.
Pop (1, 1): the closest unsettled node. Its time is final: 1. Push its neighbours: 4 at 1 + 3 = 4.
Pop (1, 3): the closest unsettled node. Its time is final: 1. Push its neighbours: 4 at 1 + 1 = 2.
Pop (2, 4): settle node 4 at time 2. No unsettled neighbours to push.
Pop (4, 4): node 4 is already settled at a shorter time. This old entry is stale — skip it.
Every node is settled. The last to hear the signal is at time 2: the answer. Node 4 was pushed twice (4 via node 1, 2 via node 3) — the heap handed out the cheaper one first.
Cheapest price from 0 to 3 with at most 1 stop. Round r allows one more flight. Start: only the source is free.
Round 1 (one flight, 0 stops). Relax every flight using LAST round's prices, written into a copy: 0→1 costs 0 + 100 = £100. 1→2 can't use that £100 yet — it was only found this round.
Round 2 (two flights, 1 stop). From last round's prices: 1→2: 100 + 100 = 200; 1→3: 100 + 600 = 700.
Stop after k + 1 = 2 rounds. Answer: £700 (0 → 1 → 3). The route 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 costs only £400, but it needs 2 stops, which is not allowed.

1-d-dynamic-programming.title: 1-D DP: each answer is built from answers already saved

frames.caption: How many ways to climb 5 steps, taking 1 or 2 at a time? Your last move onto step i came from step i − 1 or step i − 2 — so ways(i) = ways(i − 1) + ways(i − 2).

shapes.text: step i:  dp[i] = number of ways to reach step i

frames.caption: Base cases: there is 1 way to stand at step 0 (do nothing) and 1 way to reach step 1 (one small step).

shapes.text: step i:  dp[i] = number of ways to reach step i

frames.caption: dp[2] = dp[1] + dp[0] = 1 + 1 = 2. Both answers were already saved, so this costs one addition.

shapes.text: step i:  dp[i] = number of ways to reach step i

frames.caption: dp[3] = dp[2] + dp[1] = 2 + 1 = 3. Both answers were already saved, so this costs one addition.

shapes.text: step i:  dp[i] = number of ways to reach step i

frames.caption: dp[4] = dp[3] + dp[2] = 3 + 2 = 5. Both answers were already saved, so this costs one addition.

shapes.text: step i:  dp[i] = number of ways to reach step i

frames.caption: dp[5] = dp[4] + dp[3] = 5 + 3 = 8. Both answers were already saved, so this costs one addition.

shapes.text: step i:  dp[i] = number of ways to reach step i

frames.caption: Answer: 8 ways. Each step is worked out once from saved answers: O(n), instead of the O(2ⁿ) of plain recursion that keeps re-solving the same steps.

shapes.text: step i:  dp[i] = number of ways to reach step i

frames.caption: Rob houses for the most money, but never two next door. At each house there are only two choices: skip it, or rob it and give up the one before.
House 0 (£2). Skip: keep 0. Rob: 0 + 2 = 2. Keep the bigger: 2.
House 1 (£7). Skip: keep 2. Rob: 0 + 7 = 7. Keep the bigger: 7.
House 2 (£9). Skip: keep 7. Rob: best two back (2) + 9 = 11. Keep the bigger: 11.
House 3 (£3). Skip: keep 11. Rob: best two back (7) + 3 = 10. Keep the bigger: 11.
House 4 (£1). Skip: keep 11. Rob: best two back (11) + 1 = 12. Keep the bigger: 12.
Answer: £12, from houses 0, 2, 4 (2 + 9 + 1). Each house looked back only two places, so O(n) time — and O(1) space if you keep just two numbers.

2-d-dynamic-programming.title: 2-D DP: fill a table where each cell uses cells already filled

frames.caption: Count the paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of a 3 × 3 grid, moving only right or down. Each cell will hold the number of paths that reach it.
The top row and the left column can each be reached only one way (straight along the edge): 1.
Cell (1,1): you arrive from above (1 path) or from the left (1 path): 1 + 1 = 2.
Cell (1,2): you arrive from above (1 path) or from the left (2 paths): 1 + 2 = 3.
Cell (2,1): you arrive from above (2 paths) or from the left (1 path): 2 + 1 = 3.
Cell (2,2): you arrive from above (3 paths) or from the left (3 paths): 3 + 3 = 6.
Answer: 6 paths. Each cell is filled once from two saved neighbours: O(m × n).
Longest common subsequence of 'abcde' and 'ace'. Cell (i, j) holds the answer for the first i letters of one and the first j of the other. Row and column 0 are empty strings: 0.
Row 'a': it matches 'a', so that cell is the diagonal (up-left) + 1 = 1. Every other cell copies the bigger of up and left.
Row 'b': it matches no letter of 'ace', so every cell copies the bigger of up and left. Nothing new is gained.
Row 'c': it matches 'c', so that cell is the diagonal (up-left) + 1 = 2. Every other cell copies the bigger of up and left.
Row 'd': it matches no letter of 'ace', so every cell copies the bigger of up and left. Nothing new is gained.
Row 'e': it matches 'e', so that cell is the diagonal (up-left) + 1 = 3. Every other cell copies the bigger of up and left.
Answer: the corner, 3. Reading back along the diagonal steps gives the letters: 'ace'. O(m × n) cells, each filled once.

greedy.title: Greedy: make the locally best choice, and know why it is safe

frames.caption: Find the contiguous stretch with the biggest sum. Walk once, keeping a running sum of the current stretch.
Start with -2: running = -2, best = -2.
The running sum before 1 was negative — carrying it can only drag 1 down. Drop it and start fresh at 1: running = 1. New best: 1.
Add -3: running = -2. Best stays 1.
The running sum before 4 was negative — carrying it can only drag 4 down. Drop it and start fresh at 4: running = 4. New best: 4.
Add -1: running = 3. Best stays 4.
Add 2: running = 5. New best: 5.
Add 1: running = 6. New best: 6.
Add -5: running = 1. Best stays 6.
Add 4: running = 5. Best stays 6.
Answer: 6, from [4, -1, 2, 1]. The greedy rule — "a negative running sum never helps, drop it" — gives O(n) instead of checking every stretch.
Each number is the longest jump from that spot. Can you reach the last index? Greedy: just track the farthest index you can reach so far.
Index 0 can jump up to 3, reaching index 3. Farthest = max(0, 3) = 3.
Index 1 can jump up to 2, reaching index 3. Farthest = max(3, 3) = 3.
Index 2 can jump up to 1, reaching index 3. Farthest = max(3, 3) = 3.
Index 3 can jump up to 0, reaching index 3. Farthest = max(3, 3) = 3.
Index 4 is past the farthest reach (3). Every route gets stuck on the 0 at index 3. Answer: False.
No need to try every route: one pass, O(n). If the farthest reach ever gets to the last index, the answer is True instead.

intervals.title: Intervals: sort by start, then only neighbours can overlap

frames.caption: Can one person attend every meeting? Only if no two meetings overlap.
Sort by start time. Then any clash must be between neighbours in the sorted order, so one pass of neighbour checks is enough.
[0, 30] then [5, 10]: the second starts at 5, before the first ends at 30 (5 < 30). A clash: answer False.
Answer: False. Sorting costs O(n log n); the check after it is one pass.
Merge overlapping intervals. They arrive in no particular order.
Sort by start. Now an interval can only overlap the one just before it (or the merged block that one joined).
[1, 3] is the first: start the merged list with it.
[2, 6] starts at 2 ≤ 3, the end of the last merged block: they overlap. Stretch that block's end to max(3, 6) = 6.
[8, 10] starts at 8 > 6: no overlap. Add it as a new block.
[15, 18] starts at 15 > 10: no overlap. Add it as a new block.
Answer: [[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]. Sort, then one pass comparing each interval with the last merged block: O(n log n).

math-geometry.title: Math and geometry: carry digits; rotate by transpose + reverse

frames.caption: Add one to the number 199, stored as a list of digits. Work from the last digit, just like adding by hand.
Index 2: 9 + 1 = 10. Write 0 and carry 1 to the digit on the left.
Index 1: 9 + 1 = 10. Write 0 and carry 1 to the digit on the left.
Index 0: 1 + 1 = 2. No carry, so stop — the digits further left don't change.
Answer: [2, 0, 0]. Only the trailing 9s change. If every digit is 9 (like 999), all become 0 and a 1 goes in front: [1, 0, 0, 0].
Rotate the matrix 90° clockwise, in place. Each row is coloured so you can follow it: the top row must end up as the right-hand column.
Step 1: transpose — swap across the main diagonal, so row i becomes column i. Cells on the diagonal (1, 5, 9) stay put.
Swap (0,1) with (1,0): 2 and 4 trade places across the diagonal.
Swap (0,2) with (2,0): 3 and 7 trade places across the diagonal.
Swap (1,2) with (2,1): 6 and 8 trade places across the diagonal.
Step 2: reverse each row. The transpose is a mirror image of the rotation; reversing rows flips it the right way round.
Done: [[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]. The old top row (cyan) is now the right column. Every cell moved once or twice, with O(1) extra space.

bit-manipulation.title: Bits: XOR cancels pairs; shifting reuses smaller answers

frames.caption: Every number appears twice except one. XOR (^) compares bits: same bits give 0, different give 1. So x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x — pairs cancel out.
000 ^ 100 = 100. Every 1-bit of 4 flips that bit of the running value.
100 ^ 001 = 101. Every 1-bit of 1 flips that bit of the running value.
101 ^ 010 = 111. Every 1-bit of 2 flips that bit of the running value.
111 ^ 001 = 110. Every 1-bit of 1 flips that bit of the running value. 1 appeared before, so this flip undoes the earlier one.
110 ^ 010 = 100. Every 1-bit of 2 flips that bit of the running value. 2 appeared before, so this flip undoes the earlier one.
The pairs (1 and 1, 2 and 2) cancelled out; only 4 is left. Answer: 4. O(n) time and O(1) space — no hash set needed.
Count the 1-bits of every number from 0 to 5. Trick: i >> 1 drops the last bit, and that smaller number is already done. So bits(i) = bits(i >> 1) + (last bit of i).
Base case: 0 has no 1-bits.
1 = 001. Drop the last bit: 001 >> 1 = 000 = 0, which has 0. Add the last bit (1): 0 + 1 = 1.
2 = 010. Drop the last bit: 010 >> 1 = 001 = 1, which has 1. Add the last bit (0): 1 + 0 = 1.
3 = 011. Drop the last bit: 011 >> 1 = 001 = 1, which has 1. Add the last bit (1): 1 + 1 = 2.
4 = 100. Drop the last bit: 100 >> 1 = 010 = 2, which has 1. Add the last bit (0): 1 + 0 = 1.
5 = 101. Drop the last bit: 101 >> 1 = 010 = 2, which has 1. Add the last bit (1): 1 + 1 = 2.
Answer: [0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2]. Each number reuses an answer already worked out, so it is O(n) — a tiny DP on bits.
